questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: A rechargeable-lamp seller finds that buyers cannot read the charging instructions printed inside the box. Recommend one product-related response and explain how to check whether it solves the reported problem.
questions.answer: Provide clearer, accessible charging instructions with the lamp, for example larger print and labelled illustrations. Ask comparable first-time users to follow the revised instructions and record how many complete the charging steps correctly.
questions.explanation: Instructions accompanying the product affect its usability. The check should measure successful use of the instructions.

markingGuide.description: Proposes a change to the instructions supplied with the product.
Links the change to the reported reading difficulty.
Gives a practical test of whether users can follow the revised instructions.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: A bakery compares two advertisements. The first receives more online reactions, while the second produces more shop visits with a redeemable code. The campaign aims to attract paying customers. Explain why reactions alone cannot decide the winner and give one further measure the bakery should compare.
questions.answer: Reactions show interaction with the advertisement. They do not establish that someone bought bread. Compare completed purchases or contribution generated by code users, allowing for campaign spending and comparable exposure periods.
questions.explanation: The measure should connect the advertising response to the stated commercial aim.

markingGuide.description: Distinguishes engagement from completed buying.
Proposes a measure related to paying customers.
Explains a condition needed for a fair comparison.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: Customers buy a locally made raincoat because of a colourful launch campaign, but several complain that its seams let water through. The maker plans to change both the seams and the advertisement at once. Explain one reason to improve the seams and one problem with using this combined change to measure the effect of the new advertisement.
questions.answer: The seams affect the raincoat’s performance in use and should be improved to address the reported defect. Changing performance and advertising together makes it difficult to attribute a later sales change to the advertisement alone.
questions.explanation: The answer distinguishes a product intervention from a promotion intervention and considers how they affect evaluation.

markingGuide.description: Links seam quality to product performance.
Recognises that both interventions can affect buying.
Explains why their simultaneous introduction weakens attribution.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: A shoe maker adds a free size-exchange service to the offer while leaving the advertising unchanged. Which aspect of the offer is most directly improved?
questions.answer: The service attached to the product.
questions.explanation: The exchange service changes what the buyer receives as part of the product offer.
options: The wording of the existing advertisement.
The number of wholesale intermediaries.
The service attached to the product.
The price charged per advertising impression.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: A new brand of exercise books is displayed clearly in a shop, but buyers say they have never heard of it. The paper quality and price meet their needs. Which response most directly addresses the evidence?
questions.answer: Introduce targeted communication that makes the brand and its benefits known.
questions.explanation: The reported gap is awareness, which promotion can address.
options: Introduce targeted communication that makes the brand and its benefits known.
Reduce the strength of the binding.
Remove the books from the shop shelves.
Add an intermediary without communicating with buyers.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish product decisions from promotion and use customer evidence to select a response.
questions.prompt: A seller describes a small cloth sample sent to prospective buyers as a complete change in the fabric itself. Which assessment is best supported?
questions.answer: The sample can promote the existing fabric without changing the fabric’s characteristics.
questions.explanation: Sending a sample can help customers examine a product while the product stays the same.
options: Sending any sample necessarily changes the fibre composition.
A sample is always a new retail outlet.
A sample proves that every recipient will become a buyer.
The sample can promote the existing fabric without changing the fabric’s characteristics.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A trader sells a pack for ₦500. The variable cost is ₦320. During a promotion, the price would be ₦450 and there would be an additional fixed advertising cost of ₦3,000. Normal sales are 100 packs. How many whole packs must be sold during the promotion to produce at least the normal total contribution after the extra advertising cost?
questions.answer: At least 162 packs. Normal contribution is 100 × (500 − 320) = ₦18,000. Promotional contribution after advertising is 130q − 3,000. Setting this at least ₦18,000 gives q at least 21,000/130, so round up to 162.
questions.explanation: The calculation includes the lower unit contribution and the extra campaign cost. The answer is a required sales volume under the stated costs.

markingGuide.description: Finds normal total contribution of ₦18,000.
Finds promotional unit contribution of ₦130 and includes ₦3,000 advertising.
Obtains the threshold and rounds up to 162 whole packs.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A seller charges ₦2,000 for delivery of a basket in town A and ₦2,500 for the same basket delivered in town B because transport to B costs more. Another seller charges a high price to support an exclusive brand image. Identify the two pricing approaches and explain how their bases differ.
questions.answer: The first is geographical pricing based on location and delivery cost. The second is prestige pricing intended to support an exclusive image. Their stated reasons are delivery conditions and perceived positioning respectively.
questions.explanation: Classification follows the reason given for the price rather than the fact that one price is higher.

markingGuide.description: Identifies geographical pricing.
Identifies prestige pricing.
Explains the different bases for the prices.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A snack maker wants to keep a familiar ₦200 pack price as ingredient costs rise, and proposes reducing the pack from 80 g to 60 g. Identify the pricing approach, calculate the change in the price per gram, and explain one customer issue the maker should consider.
questions.answer: This follows customary pricing by holding the familiar pack price while changing quantity. The price per gram rises from ₦2.50 to ₦10/3, about ₦3.33. Customers may judge the smaller pack as poorer value, so the new quantity should be made clear.
questions.explanation: The unchanged pack price conceals a higher price for the same amount of product unless quantity is compared.

markingGuide.description: Identifies customary pricing.
Calculates both prices per gram.
Explains a relevant customer-value or clear-quantity issue.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A shop prices one essential item below its purchase cost in the hope that shoppers will also buy other goods. Which strategy best describes the stated purpose?
questions.explanation: The below-cost item is intended to attract a wider purchase basket.
options: Geographical pricing.
Loss-leader pricing.
Price lining.
Cost-plus pricing.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A clothing shop creates three distinct price levels for its shirt ranges so that customers can choose a basic, standard or premium range. Which strategy does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The seller organises related products into distinct price levels.
options: A single uniform price for every product.
A temporary below-cost offer on all goods.
Price lining.
A location-based charge for identical deliveries.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Apply pricing strategies and assess their effect on contribution and customer trial.
questions.prompt: A stationery shop sets a notebook price at ₦995 because it expects customers to perceive it differently from ₦1,000. Which strategy is most directly indicated by the stated reason?
questions.explanation: The reason concerns the buyer’s perception of the displayed number.
options: Adding a fixed percentage to production cost.
Psychological pricing.
Varying the price by delivery location.
Setting every price equal to the market leader’s.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A ceramic maker supplies retailers through a wholesaler. A retailer offers to buy directly and asks for the same discount the wholesaler receives. Explain why removing the wholesaler does not by itself show that the maker can afford this discount.
questions.answer: The maker may take over functions such as storing stock, breaking bulk, processing smaller orders and arranging delivery. Any saving in intermediary margin must be compared with the cost of those functions and the proposed discount.
questions.explanation: Channel changes redistribute work as well as margins.

markingGuide.description: Identifies a function that must still be performed.
Explains who may take it over.
Compares potential savings with replacement costs and discount.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A small printer sells customised exercise books to schools. An agent can introduce school buyers, while a retailer wants standard designs to sell from stock. Recommend a channel for highly customised orders and explain one agreement the printer should make before using it.
questions.answer: Direct selling or an agent who connects schools with the printer suits orders requiring detailed specifications. The printer should agree who confirms design, quantity, payment and delivery with the school, and how any agent is paid.
questions.explanation: Accept a channel recommendation supported by the need to communicate and confirm customised specifications.

markingGuide.description: Recommends a suitable channel.
Connects the choice to customised order requirements.
Identifies an important service or payment responsibility to agree.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A cooperative can use one distributor reaching many outlets or several retailers supplied directly. What two pieces of evidence should it collect before deciding which arrangement gives dependable service at an acceptable cost? Explain the value of each.
questions.answer: Collect the total cost of delivering and supporting each arrangement, including handling smaller orders, and records of delivery reliability or stock availability at outlets. Costs show the resources required, while service records show whether customers can obtain goods when needed.
questions.explanation: Credit other relevant evidence if it covers both the cost and service aims.

markingGuide.description: Identifies relevant total channel cost information.
Explains what that cost information establishes.
Identifies a reliability or availability measure.
Explains how the service evidence informs the decision.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A sales agent introduces a household to a furniture maker and earns commission when a sale is completed. The maker produces and delivers the furniture, and the agent does not buy it for resale. Which role is described?
questions.answer: An intermediary who arranges a sale without taking ownership of the furniture.
questions.explanation: The stated commission and absence of purchase for resale distinguish the agent’s function.
options: An intermediary who arranges a sale without taking ownership of the furniture.
A retailer buying finished furniture to resell from stock.
A consumer purchasing furniture for personal use.
A manufacturer making furniture in its own factory.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A business buys crates from a manufacturer, holds them in a warehouse and supplies smaller quantities to retailers. Which service is most clearly illustrated?
questions.answer: Breaking bulk and making stock available to retailers.
questions.explanation: The business converts large purchases into smaller supplies for retail customers.
options: Manufacturing the contents of the crates.
Removing the need for goods to be stored.
Ensuring that every retailer charges the same final price.
Breaking bulk and making stock available to retailers.

questions.subject: Marketing
questions.learningObjective: Identify channel structures and evaluate their suitability against reach, costs and service requirements.
questions.prompt: A farm begins taking household orders on its own website and delivering them from the farm. Which conclusion about its channel is best supported?
questions.answer: It sells directly while still carrying out order handling and delivery.
questions.explanation: An online order channel can remove resale intermediaries while physical distribution tasks continue.
options: Using a website automatically makes the farm a wholesaler.
Online payment removes the need to transport the produce.
It sells directly while still carrying out order handling and delivery.
Household buyers become retail intermediaries when they order online.
